_comment: YourPHR shipped defaults (#456). Flat, dotted, LOWERCASE keys; values keep their case. Do NOT edit this file to configure an instance — put only what differs in <data>/config/app-custom-config.json, which is outside git. Keys here map to env as YOURPHR_<KEY> with '.' and '-' becoming '_' (operator.contact_email -> YOURPHR_OPERATOR_CONTACT_EMAIL). Keys beginning with _ are comments and are stripped on load.
_comment_web: HTTP listener. web.listen.port is the port INSIDE the container; host.port is what docker-compose published outside it.
_comment_host: Unprefixed HOST_IP / HOST_PORT, describing how the app is reached from OUTSIDE the container. Bound explicitly because env auto-mapping only covers YOURPHR_*.
_comment_relay: SMART on FHIR OAuth relay. relay.url is where the backend POLLS /pending (may be cluster-internal); relay.public_url is the origin the PROVIDER redirects the browser to. Empty values fall back to the project relay.
_comment_metrics: Process metrics scrape server for completed sync jobs. Internal only.
_comment_storage: storage.data_dir names the directory holding everything this instance owns and must not lose: db, cache, backups, the generated JWT key, and this config's custom overlay. Empty means derive it from database.location's parent. It NEVER moves the database — see #451.
_comment_database: database.location is an absolute path inside the container. Setting it is independent of storage.data_dir. database.encryption.enabled is TRUE because that is what the image's baked config.yaml supplied for years — a stock Docker install set an encryption key at first-run and has an ENCRYPTED database, so defaulting to false would leave it unopenable (#470). Enabling encryption requires database.encryption.key and currently disables backup and restore (#367). Deployments that run unencrypted must set YOURPHR_DATABASE_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED=false explicitly.
_comment_database_encryption_key: Catalogued with an empty default so it is a KNOWN setting, not so it can be stored here — it is on the secret list, and a key written beside the database it unlocks protects nothing. Empty means 'not supplied'. Without this entry the startup unknown-key check warned that YOURPHR_DATABASE_ENCRYPTION_KEY 'has no effect', which is both false and alarming for the one variable that, if ignored, leaves the database unopenable.
_comment_backup: Scheduled backup of the database. All empty/false/0 by default. Since #545 these ARE the operator's settings: the Admin Database card saves straight into the config system (custom overlay), the ngdpbase pattern — the old .backup_settings.json side-store is migrated in once and retired. backup.allowed-roots confines where a destination may point.
_comment_jwt: jwt.issuer.key is the HS256 key signing every session — the root of trust for auth and per-user isolation. It is an ENV REFERENCE, not a value (#460): set YOURPHR_JWT_ISSUER_KEY and it is used; leave it unset and the value resolves empty, which the code reads as 'nobody set a key' and generates a random 256-bit one, persisting it to <data>/.jwt_issuer_key. So a stock install is secure with no action. Do NOT put a literal key here — this file is in git.
_comment_log: log.file empty means stdout only. log.redact_secrets makes values of type config.Secret print as [REDACTED] in logs and JSON; turning it OFF is a debugging aid for when the only way to diagnose a rejected token is to see it, and the server warns loudly on every start while it is off. Do not leave it off.
_comment_cda: C-CDA / CCD import via the external fhir-converter sidecar. ON by default because XML is what patient portals actually export, and the shipped docker-compose files start the sidecar automatically — this was the image's baked default and is preserved here (#470). The URL is the compose service name; Kubernetes deployments set YOURPHR_CDA_CONVERTER_URL, and a deployment without a sidecar sets YOURPHR_CDA_CONVERTER_ENABLED=false. Uploading XML with no reachable converter fails with an error naming what to fix; nothing else is affected.
_comment_medications: Patient-friendly medication names from the embedded (offline) RxTerms crosswalk. The API fallback makes outbound calls to RxNav, so it is off by default.
_comment_search: AI-assisted record search/chat via a Typesense index plus an external LLM (vllm-compatible endpoint). OFF by default, matching cda_converter/metrics: it depends on two services this instance may not have (a Typesense server and an LLM endpoint), so a stock install must not try to reach either. Turning it on with no reachable Typesense server fails the same way an unreachable cda-converter does: a clear error naming what to fix, nothing else affected. search.api_key is the shared secret between this backend and the Typesense server's own config (e.g. its TYPESENSE_API_KEY) — not a credential Typesense issues, so there is nothing to auto-generate; an operator enabling search must set the same value on both sides.
_comment_sync: Background refresh of provider access tokens. Set to 0 or less to disable the worker.
_comment_theme: UI theme id, served unauthenticated so it can apply before first paint. Empty means the frontend's built-in default.
_comment_bootstrap: Provision this instance's admin account at startup instead of having a human claim it through the first-run wizard (#504). OFF by default: a stock install must still show the wizard, because 'read a password out of a file' is worse for someone running docker-compose at home. Turn it ON for a provisioned deployment — the first-run wizard is a RACE on any internet-facing host, since the first account created on an empty database becomes the admin and the app cannot tell the operator from a passing stranger. NO PASSWORD IS SUPPLIED: the app generates one, writes it 0600 to <data root>/.admin_bootstrap_password, and logs the PATH only. That keeps the credential out of cluster secrets, .env files, CI logs and release images, makes it unique per instance, and rotates it whenever the database is rebuilt. The file is deleted after the admin's first successful sign-in, because the data root is exactly what a backup contains (#466). Provisioning is one-way: only ever on an empty user table, never overwriting an account or changing a password. These are catalogued so the startup unknown-key check does not flag them, but they are BOOTSTRAP — set them in the environment, not the config store (#472), because they must work before any admin exists to open the config screen.
_comment_bootstrap_seed: Install the demo database baked into the release image when this instance has no database yet (#505), so a public demo comes up already populated and a reset is 'delete the file and restart'. OFF by default and DEMO-ONLY: a normal install must never come up holding synthetic patient records. The seed contains the shared demo account and NO admin — the image is public, so a baked admin credential would be a published one, identical on every deployment — which is why restoring REFUSES unless bootstrap.admin.enabled is also set: otherwise the instance would start populated, reachable, and administrable by nobody, with the first-run wizard suppressed because users exist. Restore happens before the database is opened and never over an existing database. Bootstrap, so set it in the environment (#472).
_comment_trusted_proxies: Which proxies may tell us the client's address (#529). CIDRs or bare addresses, e.g. ["10.42.0.0/16"] for a k3s pod network or ["172.18.0.1"] for a single docker gateway. EMPTY MEANS TRUST NOTHING, and that is the default: forwarding headers are ignored and the client address is the actual socket peer. Gin's own default is the opposite — it trusts EVERY proxy (0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0), which makes X-Forwarded-For caller-controlled, so any client can choose its own identity. That is not merely cosmetic: web.rate_limit.auth_per_minute below keys on c.ClientIP(), so rotating the header lands in a fresh bucket on every request and the brute-force backstop never fires. Both directions are wrong in different ways — set this too broadly and a client picks its own address; leave it unset behind a reverse proxy and every client shares the proxy's bucket, which is one reason #509 added a per-ACCOUNT limit that does not depend on the source address at all. An unparseable entry is logged and leaves the server trusting nothing, because a typo must not silently restore trust-everything.
_comment_rate_limit: Per-IP fixed-window cap on the UNAUTHENTICATED credential endpoints (signup, signin), to blunt online password guessing (#104). 10/minute is a brute-force backstop, not a throughput setting — bcrypt already makes each attempt expensive. Catalogued because 10 is too low for an automated suite driving real logins: the E2E harness makes ~16 auth calls from one IP and was silently getting 429s that the UI rendered as 'username or password is incorrect', which read as a login regression (#481). Raise it for a test instance; leave it alone in production. NOTE the limiter keys on c.ClientIP(): whether that value can be trusted depends entirely on web.trusted_proxies above (#529). Behind a proxy listed there, every client correctly gets its own bucket; with the list empty behind a proxy, all clients share one — which is also why #509 added a per-ACCOUNT limit that does not depend on the source address. Set to 0 or less to disable the per-IP limit; the server logs a warning on every start while it is off.
_comment_rate_limit_account: Failed sign-ins allowed per USERNAME per window (#509), counted in addition to the per-IP limit above. The two cover opposite holes: per-IP alone never throttles a slow distributed attempt against one account (a few tries from each of many addresses stays under every bucket while hammering one username indefinitely), and per-IP alone makes a household throttle ITSELF, because everyone behind one NAT address shares a bucket. ONLY FAILURES COUNT — counting successes would throttle a legitimately busy account, and a success-counting limiter is what made the E2E suite look like a login regression in #481. A refusal is the same generic 429 whether or not the username exists: telling an attacker that an account is being throttled is itself enumeration (#104). NOT account lockout, which #507 rejected — lockout is a denial-of-service weapon against the account owner. Set to 0 or less to disable this limit.
_comment_rate_limit_window: The window both auth limits are measured over. One key so they cannot drift apart — before this the per-IP window was a hardcoded time.Minute at the call site while its limit was configuration, which meant the name of the limit key was only accidentally true. A non-positive value falls back to 60 seconds rather than disabling anything: an unusable window is a typo, and reading it as 'turn the brute-force backstop off' is the wrong direction to guess in. Disabling is what the two LIMIT keys are for.
_comment_password_policy: Rules a NEW or CHANGED password must satisfy (#506). Enforced SERVER-SIDE by signup, admin user-create and change-password — the browser forms read these same values and are a courtesy, not the control. Deliberately NOT applied at SIGN-IN: an account created before a policy existed, or before an operator raised the minimum, must still be able to get in; validating a password someone already has locks them out of their own records to enforce a rule they cannot act on until they are inside. Length is measured in BYTES because bcrypt's limit is a byte limit and UTF-8 is variable width — an emoji is four bytes, so a 20-character passphrase can be 80 bytes. NO COMPOSITION RULES (one uppercase, one digit, one symbol) and none are planned: NIST SP 800-63B recommends against them because they push people toward `Password1!` and into reuse while adding little entropy. Length plus a breached-password check is the current guidance.
_comment_password_max_length: bcrypt refuses anything over 72 BYTES with ErrPasswordTooLong, which would otherwise reach a user pasting a passphrase out of a password manager as a raw internal error. 69 leaves a small margin under that ceiling; configuration above 72 is clamped rather than honoured, because the limit belongs to the algorithm and not to the operator.
_comment_password_deny: deny_common rejects the handful of passwords tried FIRST in every credential-stuffing run, from a short embedded list — not the Pwned Passwords API, which would add an outbound network call to sign-up and tell a third party that somebody just set a password here; unacceptable for a self-hosted PHR that has to work with no internet (see #507). deny_username rejects a password containing the account name.
_comment_username_policy: Minimum username length (#506). One value, so the sign-in form, the sign-up form and the server stop disagreeing — before this the sign-in page enforced 2 while telling the user 4, and sign-up enforced 4, so the sign-in page rejected usernames the server had happily created. Published so the forms derive their validators from it rather than hardcoding a number that drifts. Reserved names are a separate rule and live in the repository (#519), because that one applies to self-service registration rather than to every account.
_comment_signup: Self-service account creation (#498). TRUE by default, which is the behaviour every install has always had — there was no gate at all before this key. Turn it OFF on an internet-facing instance so strangers cannot create accounts; an operator still adds family members from Admin -> Users, so closing signup removes self-service, not multi-user support. THE FIRST RUN IGNORES THIS FLAG: with an empty user table AuthSignup proceeds whatever this says, because the first account created is the instance OWNER and gets UserRoleAdmin, and it is the only way an admin ever comes into existence — no seeded admin, no CLI user-create, no password reset. A flag that could block it would make a fresh deployment unadministrable. On the `public` list so the sign-in page can hide 'Create an Account' rather than offer a link that fails.
_comment_demo: Public demo mode (#495). OFF by default: turning it on puts a one-click sign-in for a SHARED account on the sign-in page, which is only ever appropriate for a throwaway instance holding synthetic records. demo.enabled is on the `public` list so the sign-in page can read it with no login. On a public instance this MUST be paired with the connect guard (#496): the demo account is shared, so a visitor who can connect a real provider puts a real person's records in front of the next visitor.
_comment_demo_admin: A second one-click entrance that signs a visitor in as an admin who can SEE everything and CHANGE nothing (#516), so a reviewer or a prospective self-hoster can look at Configuration, Users, Database and Logs without an operator handing out a real admin credential. OFF by default and only meaningful with demo.enabled. The account is provisioned at startup with a generated password nobody knows, exactly like demo.password (#515). READ-ONLY IS ENFORCED SERVER-SIDE, DEFAULT-DENY: for this account the API allows GET plus a short list of read-only POSTs and refuses everything else, so a route added later is blocked by inheritance rather than by somebody remembering — which is precisely how #514 happened. Two GETs are refused as well: revealing a secret configuration value, and browsing the server's directories. A hidden button is not a control; these routes answer curl.
_comment_demo_reset: Reset this instance to the demo database baked into the image on every start (#518). OFF by default, and it is the ONLY setting in this product that deliberately destroys a live database — so it is armed by three switches together (demo.enabled, bootstrap.seed.restore, and this) and then still has to PROVE the database it is about to delete belongs to a demo: the existing accounts must all be demo.username, demo.admin.username or bootstrap.admin.username, or the reset is refused and the instance starts normally with its data intact. Encrypted databases are refused outright, because the proof cannot be read. A reset also drops the cache (derived, keyed to source IDs that will not exist) and the generated JWT signing key (otherwise tokens minted before the reset still verify against users that are gone, and a returning visitor gets errors instead of a sign-in page). The instance's custom config file is deliberately KEPT, so a reset does not unconfigure the demo.
_comment_demo_password: NOT SET BY HAND (#515). demo.password is generated per instance at startup, set on the demo account, and written here — nobody chooses it, nobody types it, and it is never published. POST /api/auth/demo-signin posts no credentials, so a visitor never needs to know one; the only thing a human-chosen value ever bought was the ability to type it at the login form, and it cost us a seed whose published password was too short for our own form (#505) and a collision with the password policy in #506. It is on the `secret` list, so it is masked on the Admin Configuration screen and never served by /api/instance/public. THE VERIFY IS THE POINT: demo-signin checks this value against the stored hash rather than minting a token for whoever demo.username names, so demo.enabled flipped on an instance that happens to hold a user called `demo` does nothing at all. Provisioning regenerates whenever the two drift apart, which is what a freshly restored seed looks like — so a reset needs no operator step.
_comment_public_password_policy: The password policy is on the list below so the sign-up form builds its validators from what the server actually enforces, instead of hardcoding numbers that drift (#506). Sizes and booleans only — the minimum length tells an attacker nothing they would not learn from one rejected attempt, while NOT publishing it is exactly what produced a form and a server that disagreed.
_comment_public: Keys served by GET /api/instance/public to callers with NO login (#457). Direction matters: this is an allow-list, so a key added anywhere else in this file is private until it is named here. A deny-list would publish anything nobody remembered to list. An instance may change this array in <data>/config/app-custom-config.json — including adding keys — and the server logs a WARN naming anything promoted beyond this shipped set. NOTE operator.contact_email is deliberately absent (#459): an address on an unauthenticated endpoint gets harvested. Signed-in users still see it via GET /api/secure/instance, and an operator running a public help desk can add it back here.
_comment_secret: Keys masked on the Admin Configuration screen until an admin explicitly reveals one (#458). Deliberately SHORT: masking 47 of 51 settings — which is what happens if everything outside `public` is hidden — makes an operator click through the listen port and the log level, and trains them to reveal reflexively. Note this list is the OPPOSITE shape to `public` and that is intentional: `public` is an allow-list because a mistake there exposes a value to the internet, while this is a deny-list because a mistake here shows a value to an already-authenticated admin on their own screen. Different consequence, different safe default. Entries need not exist in this file — listing a key that is env-only is harmless and future-proofs it.
_comment_mail: Outbound email (#524). OFF by default and CONSOLE by default, which together mean a fresh instance never sends anything and never fails trying — a message with nowhere to go is written to the log instead. That matters twice over here: the public demo must not email strangers, and development and the E2E suite need no relay at all. Design and the provider table below are adapted from jwilleke/ngdpbase docs/admin/email-setup.md, which solved the same problem for a wiki; SMTP is the stable part, so only the transport differs (Go net/smtp rather than nodemailer). Set provider to "smtp" AND enabled to true before anything leaves the instance. NOTE mail from a home IP is usually dropped or spam-filed, so in practice mail.smtp.host points at a relay the operator already has: smtp.resend.com (user "resend", pass = API key), smtp.sendgrid.net (user "apikey"), smtp.gmail.com (requires a Google APP PASSWORD, not the account password), region-specific AWS SES (IAM SMTP credentials, not AWS keys), or localhost:1025 for Mailhog in development. Sending from your own domain also needs SPF, DKIM and DMARC records or recipients will reject it.
_comment_mail_smtp: SMTP relay settings, used when mail.provider is "smtp". Port 587 with secure=false is STARTTLS and is what almost every relay wants; port 465 with secure=true is implicit TLS. mail.smtp.pass is a CREDENTIAL and is listed in `secret` below, so it is masked on the Admin Configuration screen and never served to a browser — prefer an API key scoped to sending over a full account password. There is deliberately no option to skip certificate verification: on a wiki that is a development convenience, but this channel would carry medical records, and a PHR that quietly accepts any certificate is worse than one that refuses to send.
_comment_operator: Who runs this instance. Shown on /contact. Set from Admin Dashboard -> Instance; the operator is the data controller for the records held here.
